title: Vertebrobasilar Insufficiency -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Vertebrobasilar insufficiency (VBI) is characterized by inadequate perfusion of the posterior cerebral circulation, primarily supplied by the paired vertebral arteries that converge to form the basilar artery. The posterior circulation supplies critical structures, including the brainstem, thalamus, hippocampus, cerebellum, occipital lobes, and medial temporal lobes. Etiologies of VBI include atherosclerotic stenosis, arterial dissection, embolism, and, less commonly, congenital anomalies. Risk factors parallel those of cerebrovascular disease, including advanced age, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, and smoking.

title: Vertebrobasilar Insufficiency -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Impaired posterior circulation results in clinical manifestations such as dizziness, ataxia, visual disturbances, dysarthria, and cranial nerve deficits. The condition must be differentiated from subclavian steal, bow hunter’s syndrome, labyrinthitis, vestibular neuritis, and benign paroxysmal positional vertigo.

title: Vertebrobasilar Insufficiency -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Diagnosis is established through thorough clinical evaluation, complemented by imaging studies that include magnetic resonance angiography or computed tomography angiography. Management focuses on addressing underlying vascular pathology, antithrombotic therapy, and risk factor modification, with surgical or endovascular intervention in selected cases. Complications include posterior circulation stroke and persistent neurologic deficits. The prognosis depends on timely diagnosis and effective management of vascular risk factors.

title: Vertebrobasilar Insufficiency -- Continuing Education Activity
content: This activity for healthcare professionals is designed to enhance learners' proficiency in evaluating and managing VBI. title: Vertebrobasilar Insufficiency -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Objectives: Identify the clinical and diagnostic features of vertebrobasilar insufficiency, correlating deficits with posterior circulation territories for accurate diagnosis. Select appropriate diagnostic tests, including imaging and laboratory workup, to confirm vertebrobasilar insufficiency and establish potential underlying causes, guiding timely and targeted management. Implement evidence-based, individualized approaches for managing vertebrobasilar insufficiency and mitigate its possible sequelae. Collaborate with all members of the interprofessional team, including specialists such as emergency physicians, neurologists, and neurosurgeons, to provide efficient, comprehensive, and coordinated care for patients with vertebrobasilar insufficiency. Access free multiple choice questions on this topic.

title: Vertebrobasilar Insufficiency -- Introduction
content: The vertebrobasilar system, also termed the "posterior circulation," constitutes a critical vascular network supplying the brainstem, cerebellum, thalamus, occipital lobes, and medial temporal lobes. This vascular territory accounts for approximately 20% of total cerebral arterial perfusion (see Image . Vertebral Artery Vascular Territory). The posterior circulation originates from the vertebral arteries, which typically arise from the subclavian arteries located just inferior to the clavicle. These arteries ascend through the transverse foramina of the cervical vertebrae and converge at the pontomedullary junction to form the basilar artery.

title: Vertebrobasilar Insufficiency -- Introduction
content: The common carotid (CCAs) and vertebral arteries collectively deliver roughly 15% of cardiac output to the brain, with an approximate 4:1 contribution ratio, respectively. In most individuals, vertebral arteries arise bilaterally from the subclavian arteries. The right CCA and right subclavian artery branch from the innominate (brachiocephalic) artery, which measures less than 5 cm in length and 1.2 cm in diameter, whereas the left CCA and left subclavian artery emerge from the distal aortic arch. Blood flow and vessel diameter decrease progressively from the ascending to the descending aorta (see Image . Hemodynamic Features of the Aortic Arch and Its Branches). [1] [2]

title: Vertebrobasilar Insufficiency -- Introduction
content: The transverse foramina, present exclusively in the cervical vertebrae, function as protective tunnels for the vertebral arteries as they ascend toward the cranium. Conventionally, the course of each vertebral artery from its origin at the subclavian artery is divided into 4 anatomic segments, as follows: V1: Extends from the subclavian artery to the transverse foramen of C6. V2: Courses through the foramina from C6 to C1. V3: Passes between the sulcus and the foramen magnum. V4: Represents the intradural segment.

title: Vertebrobasilar Insufficiency -- Introduction
content: The vertebral arteries converge at the pontomedullary junction to form the basilar artery, which courses along the ventral surface of the pons and bifurcates into the posterior cerebral arteries (PCAs) at the pontomesencephalic junction. The basilar artery gives rise to several major branches, including the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA), which supplies the inferior cerebellum and lateral medulla; the anterior inferior and superior cerebellar arteries, which supply the cerebellum and brainstem; and the PCAs, which supply the occipital cortex and inferomedial temporal lobes.

title: Vertebrobasilar Insufficiency -- Introduction
content: Transient ischemic attack (TIA) is defined as a temporary reduction in cerebral blood flow producing stroke-like symptoms that resolve spontaneously without resulting in infarction or diffusion-weighted imaging hyperintensity within a specific vascular territory. Vertebrobasilar insufficiency (VBI) refers specifically to a transient interruption of flow within the posterior circulation and is not confined to a single vascular territory.

title: Vertebrobasilar Insufficiency -- Etiology
content: Traditional risk factors associated with atherosclerosis are also relevant to VBI and include smoking, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, male sex, family history of vascular disease, and hyperlipidemia. The clinical diagnosis of VBI is more frequently observed in older adults due to reduced intraluminal velocity, decreased arteriole elasticity, and progressive arteriosclerosis. [13] A history of coronary or peripheral artery disease confers increased risk. [14] Other etiologies include cardioembolic conditions such as atrial fibrillation and infective endocarditis, vertebral artery dissection, systemic hypercoagulable states, and structural factors such as acquired uncovertebral (Luschka joint) hypertrophy or congenital malformations of the transverse foramina. [15] [16]

title: Vertebrobasilar Insufficiency -- Epidemiology
content: Approximately 1/4 of strokes and TIAs occur within the vertebrobasilar distribution, and up to 5% of adults older than 60 presenting with dizziness have VBI. Although many cases of dizziness are nonvascular in origin, individuals with underlying susceptibility are at increased risk of progression to disabling stroke. [17] [18] [19] Similar to other stroke syndromes, Americans of African ancestry demonstrate a higher prevalence of VBI compared with other ethnic groups, attributable to genetic and epigenetic factors, increased prevalence of hypertension, and disparities in healthcare access and delivery. [20]

title: Vertebrobasilar Insufficiency -- Pathophysiology
content: In most cases, VBI arises from ischemic changes driven by either hemodynamic insufficiency or embolism. The vertebral arteries are less commonly involved in embolism than the carotid circulation. Potential embolic sources include the aortic arch, the origin of the vertebral artery, and the proximal subclavian arteries. However, the majority of cases result from atherosclerotic disease.

title: Vertebrobasilar Insufficiency -- Pathophysiology -- Hemodynamic Causes
content: Reduced perfusion is the primary cause of VBI, particularly among older adults and individuals with diabetes, who often have impaired autonomic regulation. Symptoms are often reproducible and transient. Hemodynamic ischemia requires impaired perfusion in both vertebral arteries or within the basilar artery, due to the high density of perforating vessels in this region, coupled with limited contribution from the carotid circulation via the posterior communicating arteries of the circle of Willis. Additional factors that may reduce perfusion include antihypertensive therapy, cardiac dysrhythmias, pacemaker malfunction, and vasculitis. Occlusions in other vessels, such as those seen in subclavian steal syndrome, can also divert blood from the brainstem, producing VBI.

title: Vertebrobasilar Insufficiency -- Pathophysiology -- Embolic Mechanisms
content: Embolic VBI arises from atherosclerotic plaques that dislodge as emboli or intimal defects that result from trauma, compression, fibromuscular dysplasia, aneurysm, or dissection. Most extracranial lesions originate from atherosclerotic buildup within a vertebral artery and, rarely, the innominate or subclavian arteries. In some cases, thrombi may form in dolichoectasia or fusiform basilar artery aneurysms and subsequently embolize to distal branches. [21] [22] [23]

title: Vertebrobasilar Insufficiency -- History and Physical
content: A thorough history is essential for the evaluation of VBI, with particular attention to cardiovascular risk factors such as atherosclerosis and advanced age. Assessment should emphasize neurologic and cardiogenic causes, as symptoms reflect ischemia in regions supplied by the posterior circulation. Many manifestations of VBI may mimic nonvascular conditions, including labyrinthitis, vestibular neuritis, and benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV). Notably, reproducible symptoms elicited by positional head changes or extension are of diagnostic significance. [24] [25]

title: Vertebrobasilar Insufficiency -- History and Physical
content: The most common symptom of VBI is dizziness or vertigo. Near-syncope occurs in approximately 60% of patients, often presenting as transient lightheadedness or fainting. Other manifestations include sudden “drop attacks” characterized by abrupt weakness in the knees, diplopia or vision loss—such as occurs in hairdresser syndrome from neck hyperextension—paresthesia, hand claudication, and dysarthria. [26] [27]

title: Vertebrobasilar Insufficiency -- History and Physical
content: Headache may also be present and can mimic posterior migraines, particularly with PCA involvement. [28] Altered consciousness may result from ischemia of the reticular formation, while ataxia reflects involvement of cerebellar-vestibular tracts.

title: Vertebrobasilar Insufficiency -- History and Physical
content: Contralateral motor weakness indicates compromise of the pyramidal tracts, and loss of temperature or pain sensation suggests medullary or sympathetic tract ischemia. Additional features may include urinary incontinence secondary to pontine micturition center involvement and abrupt hearing loss associated with anterior inferior cerebellar artery perfusion deficits in the labyrinthine artery. [29]

title: Vertebrobasilar Insufficiency -- History and Physical
content: Neurologic deficits arising from VBI include changes in level of consciousness, hemiparesis, and alterations in pupillary size and reactivity. Cranial nerve involvement may manifest as abducens (cranial nerve VI) palsy, vertical gaze palsy due to oculomotor (cranial nerve III) dysfunction, facial nerve (cranial nerve VII) paralysis, or bulbar palsy presenting with dysarthria, dysphonia, dysphagia, and facial weakness. Additional findings include contralateral hemianopia with macular sparing from PCA involvement and ipsilateral temperature loss and facial pain consistent with Horner syndrome as part of medullary syndrome.

title: Vertebrobasilar Insufficiency -- History and Physical
content: Care must be taken to exclude more benign conditions such as labyrinthitis, vestibular neuritis, and BPPV. Although vertigo is a common symptom of VBI, it is also a hallmark of peripheral vestibular disorders, which account for 80% to 90% of emergency department visits for vertiginous symptoms. Vertigo alone cannot establish a diagnosis of TIA or VBI. However, vertigo accompanied by brainstem signs is strongly indicative of VBI.

title: Vertebrobasilar Insufficiency -- History and Physical
content: Physical examination, particularly the HINTS+ protocol (head impulse, nystagmus, test of skew, and assessment for hearing loss and ataxia), is critical for identifying brainstem and cerebellar involvement in the acute setting. The presence of contralateral monoparesis or hemiparesis further supports the diagnosis, and specific patterns of nystagmus, such as vertical or direction-changing nystagmus, are indicative of central pathology. Evaluation should also consider upper cervical radiculopathy and nonconvulsive seizures that may mimic VBI. [30] [31]

title: Vertebrobasilar Insufficiency -- Evaluation
content: Digital subtraction cerebral angiography remains the gold standard for diagnosing VBI. Less invasive imaging modalities are frequently employed, including computed tomography angiography (CTA), magnetic resonance angiography (MRA), and duplex ultrasonography. CTA provides a 3-dimensional reconstruction of the intracranial and extracranial vessels. [32] For time-of-flight or pointwise encoding time reduction with radial acquisition (PETRA) MRA, contrast enhancement with gadolinium may be required for extracranial vessels to minimize swallowing artifacts. However, routine MRA may fail to detect abnormalities in patients with a clinical diagnosis of VBI. [33]

title: Vertebrobasilar Insufficiency -- Evaluation
content: CTA carries risks related to radiation exposure and nephrotoxicity of iodinated contrast. Rarely, gadolinium-based magnetic resonance contrast induces nephrogenic systemic fibrosis, also referred to as "nephrogenic fibrosing dermopathy," in patients with impaired renal function. Visualization of the V1 and V2 segments of the vertebral arteries is challenging. However, duplex ultrasonography can identify alterations in flow velocity within the proximal vertebral arteries.

title: Vertebrobasilar Insufficiency -- Evaluation
content: Modern imaging techniques are increasingly accessible and include quantitative MRA for assessing flow and guiding arterial-arterial bypass, as well as intraoperative indocyanine green videoangiography to confirm vascular perfusion. [34] [35] Additional modalities, such as dual-energy computed tomography (CT), spectral CT, arterial spin labeling, vessel wall imaging with black-blood magnetic resonance imaging, and machine learning-based analyses, further expand the repertoire of diagnostic tools.

title: Vertebrobasilar Insufficiency -- Evaluation
content: Serum analysis should encompass complete blood count, electrolytes, renal and liver function, coagulation profile, and lipid panel. In patients younger than 45 years, evaluation should also include lupus anticoagulants, anti-cardiolipin antibodies, and assessment of protein C and S activity and factor V Leiden mutation. Elevated γ-glutamyl transferase levels have been correlated with VBI and may serve as a biomarker of posterior circulation inflammation and atherosclerosis. [36]

title: Vertebrobasilar Insufficiency -- Evaluation
content: Electrocardiography may reveal ischemic changes, arrhythmias such as atrial fibrillation, or evolving myocardial infarction. Approximately 12% of patients admitted for acute ischemic stroke or TIA develop concomitant myocardial infarction within the first 3 days of hospitalization. In younger patients, transthoracic echocardiography with bubble study is recommended to exclude vegetations, valvular defects, right-to-left shunts, or floating aortic thrombi.

title: Vertebrobasilar Insufficiency -- Treatment / Management
content: The 1st-line treatment of VBI consists of antiplatelet therapy. Anticoagulation with a direct oral factor Xa inhibitor is indicated when embolic etiology is determined to be cardiogenic, provided the patient has no contraindications, such as valvular heart disease. Studies have demonstrated that betahistine hydrochloride can improve arterial hemodynamics, cerebral perfusion, and clinical outcomes in patients with VBI. [37]

title: Vertebrobasilar Insufficiency -- Treatment / Management
content: Surgical intervention is the next option for patients unresponsive to medical therapy. Endovascular approaches have largely supplanted open endarterectomy due to high perioperative mortality and complication rates. [38]

title: Vertebrobasilar Insufficiency -- Treatment / Management
content: In the acute setting, symptoms are often dependent on cerebral perfusion pressure. Perfusion may require augmentation with isotonic intravenous fluids, such as normal saline or lactated Ringer solution, and hypotension should be avoided. Intravenous fibrinolysis is effective if administered within 4.5 hours of persistent ischemic symptoms, with the window potentially extending to 24 hours in patients with mild symptoms and appropriate imaging confirming a limited infarct core. [39] [40] Although anticoagulation may be considered, current evidence does not support improved outcomes.

title: Vertebrobasilar Insufficiency -- Treatment / Management
content: Strict blood pressure control is essential in preventing secondary strokes. As with other ischemic events, secondary prevention of VBI requires a multimodal approach, including blood pressure regulation, smoking cessation, glycemic control, administration of high-intensity statins, dietary modification, and routine physical activity. [41] Surgical options are limited, depending primarily on plaque location and the feasibility of repair. [42] Indications for surgical intervention include the following: High-grade bilateral vertebral artery stenosis, defined as greater than 60% stenosis in both arteries, or greater than 60% stenosis in the dominant vertebral artery when the contralateral artery is hypoplastic, terminates in the PICA, or is occluded. Symptomatic embolism originating from a vertebral artery lesion. Symptomatic repair of an aneurysm or aneurysms exceeding 1.5 cm, regardless of symptoms.

title: Vertebrobasilar Insufficiency -- Treatment / Management
content: Two primary surgical approaches exist: open surgical repair and endovascular treatment. Open repair may involve bypass grafting of the stenosed segment or direct arterial transposition connecting the affected artery to a nearby healthy vessel. [43] Endovascular repair is more commonly performed and involves stent placement via a femoral catheter. [44] Angioplasty may be employed for basilar artery stenosis, although its role in vertebral artery stroke is poorly defined.

title: Vertebrobasilar Insufficiency -- Treatment / Management
content: Treatment of VBI is complex, and over the years, surgical techniques have evolved to become more minimally invasive, achieve improved outcomes with shorter operative times, and enhance cost-effectiveness. Traditionally, carotid endarterectomy was frequently performed in these patients, with reported 5-year survival rates of 67.6%. [45] In contrast, endovascular repair demonstrates a success rate of approximately 93%, particularly in recent decades, as advances in techniques, including closed-cell, self-expandable Carotid Wallstents, have optimized outcomes for VBI patients. [46] [47] [48]

title: Vertebrobasilar Insufficiency -- Treatment / Management
content: Anterior cervical approaches, such as discectomies and corpectomies performed for trauma or degenerative disease, carry the risk of injuring an aberrant vertebral artery during lateral displacement or retraction of the longus colli muscles. Therefore, preoperative evaluation of the posterior vasculature with head and neck CTA is recommended to minimize vascular injury.

title: Vertebrobasilar Insufficiency -- Differential Diagnosis
content: The clinical presentation of VBI can resemble numerous central and peripheral disorders, necessitating careful differentiation to ensure accurate diagnosis. These disorders include the following: BPPV Labyrinthitis Multiple sclerosis Posterior fossa tumor Subclavian steal syndrome (SSS) Ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke Anterior territory TIA Transtentorial herniation Vertebral artery dissection Vasculitis Vestibular neuronitis

content: Recognition of conditions that resemble VBI ensures that interventions are correctly targeted and timely. A structured diagnostic approach, integrating clinical assessment and selective imaging, facilitates informed management decisions.

title: Vertebrobasilar Insufficiency -- Differential Diagnosis -- Clinical Distinction Between Vertebrobasilar Insufficiency and Hemispheric Stroke
content: The clinical diagnosis of VBI is challenging due to overlapping symptoms between anterior and posterior circulation events. [49] However, 3 distinguishing features help differentiate VBI from anterior territory TIA, as follows: Both vertebral arteries generally must be compromised for symptoms to manifest because of collateral circulation through the circle of Willis, basilar artery, leptomeningeal and dural arteriolar anastomoses, and the anterior spinal artery. [50] Symptomatic vertebral artery stenosis typically presents with low flow velocities on duplex imaging, in contrast to the high velocities seen in carotid stenosis. Stenosis confers an elevated risk of recurrent vertebrobasilar stroke within 90 days, particularly during the first few weeks.

title: Vertebrobasilar Insufficiency -- Differential Diagnosis -- Clinical Distinction Between Vertebrobasilar Insufficiency and Hemispheric Stroke
content: VBI exhibits a characteristic symptom constellation: nausea, vertigo, nystagmus, cerebellar signs such as ataxia and dysmetria, ipsilateral cranial nerve deficits with contralateral corticospinal involvement, dysphagia, dysarthria, and occipital lobe-related visuospatial or visual field deficits. Cognitive impairment and aphasia are generally absent, further distinguishing posterior circulation events from hemispheric strokes.

title: Vertebrobasilar Insufficiency -- Differential Diagnosis -- Differentiating Vertebrobasilar Insufficiency From Subclavian Steal Syndrome
content: VBI and SSS may present with similar symptoms, but their hemodynamics differ. In VBI, significant stenosis of the vertebral and basilar arteries reduces anterograde blood flow. In SSS, blood is diverted from the vertebral artery to supply a stenosed or occluded subclavian artery proximal to the vertebral origin. [51] Not all individuals with SSS are symptomatic. Manifestations typically arise when collateral circulation fails to meet increased demand, such as during exercise. [52]

title: Vertebrobasilar Insufficiency -- Differential Diagnosis -- Differentiating Vertebrobasilar Insufficiency From Subclavian Steal Syndrome
content: Approximately 2/3 of patients with SSS exhibit VBI-like symptoms, including dizziness, blurred vision, syncope, or weakness. Distinguishing features of SSS include a higher prevalence in patients with coronary artery bypass grafting, reversal of vertebral artery flow on Doppler ultrasonography, dysphagia lusoria from a Kommerell diverticulum in aberrant right subclavian artery syndrome, ipsilateral arm claudication with activity, syncope, and positive provocative Adson or Allen tests.

title: Vertebrobasilar Insufficiency -- Differential Diagnosis -- Rotational Vertebral Artery Insufficiency
content: Also known as bow hunter’s syndrome, rotational vertebral artery insufficiency is an uncommon cause of VBI that occurs during head rotation secondary to vertebral artery compression by atlantoaxial pathology at C1-C2 or below C2. In most cases, symptomatic presentation requires the coexistence of bilateral pathology, such as a hypoplastic or severely atherosclerotic contralateral vertebral artery, or a vertebral artery terminating in the PICA rather than the basilar artery. [53]

title: Vertebrobasilar Insufficiency -- Prognosis
content: The rate of stroke recurrence after VBI is approximately 25% within 90 days, and mortality from ischemic strokes in the vertebrobasilar system is twice that observed in the carotid circulation. [54] [55] Endovascular interventions, including the use of combined balloon-mounted and self-expanding stents, have the potential to reduce the 30-day incidence of stroke, TIA, and death to less than 5%.

title: Vertebrobasilar Insufficiency -- Prognosis
content: The Wingspan Stent System Postmarket Surveillance Study (WEAVE trial) demonstrated low periprocedural complication rates associated with stent placement in intracranial arteries. The China Angioplasty and Stenting for Symptomatic Intracranial Severe Stenosis (CASSISS) trial found no significant difference in the 30-day risk of stroke or death between medical therapy alone and medical therapy combined with stenting for severe symptomatic intracranial artery stenosis. Together, these trials support the safety profile of endovascular intervention for VBI. [56] [57] [58]

title: Vertebrobasilar Insufficiency -- Complications
content: Patients with VBI are at risk for a range of secondary complications due to immobility, reduced perfusion, and associated comorbidities. These complications can include deep vein thrombosis, aspiration pneumonia, myocardial infarction, pulmonary embolism, pressure sores, and gastritis. Recognition and early management of these complications are critical to improving patient outcomes.

title: Vertebrobasilar Insufficiency -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Primary care clinicians and patients should understand that the symptoms of VBI are often common and nonspecific, with dizziness, vertigo, nausea, and vomiting being particularly frequent. Patients with underlying vascular risk factors should be educated on the importance of seeking urgent medical attention when these symptoms occur, particularly if accompanied by brainstem signs such as dysarthria, diplopia, or impaired coordination.

title: Vertebrobasilar Insufficiency -- Pearls and Other Issues
content: Recognizing the clinical distinctions between peripheral vestibular disorders and central disorders caused by VBI is essential. The presence of brainstem signs, including dysarthria, diplopia, ataxia, or cranial nerve deficits, should prompt consideration of VBI. Bedside HINTS testing is a critical clinical tool for evaluation.

title: Vertebrobasilar Insufficiency -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: VBI management requires an interprofessional team, including emergency department clinicians, neurology, neurosurgery, interventional neuroradiology, and internal medicine specialists. A vascular neurologist guides definitive treatment, while primary care practitioners play a key role in educating patients on secondary prevention and minimizing modifiable risk factors. At minimum, patients should be advised to abstain from smoking, adhere to prescribed medications, maintain a healthy body weight, achieve a low-density lipoprotein cholesterol target below 70 mg/dL, and engage in regular physical activity. Given the risk of recurrent stroke, close longitudinal surveillance is essential. Speech, occupational, physical, and vestibular rehabilitation form an integral component of poststroke and post-VBI care.
